problem: Prior multi-modal fusion for language-conditioned navigation (concatenation, Gated-Attention Hadamard product) either fails in one of 2D/3D settings, converges slowly, or generalizes poorly to unseen instructions.
motivation: Grounding language in perception and action requires an agent to recognise objects, remember them, decompose the instruction and navigate around distractors. The authors want a compact, end-to-end trainable fusion of visual and textual features that works across 2D and 3D and gives zero-shot generalization.
key_idea: Project the GRU sentence embedding through n parallel FC layers, use each vector as a 1x1 convolution filter over the CNN feature map to get n attention maps, and feed only the stacked maps to an A3C policy.
insight: Discarding the visual features and keeping only the stacked attention maps works best: the variant that concatenates an attention map with the visual features (A3C_netattn) collapses to SR 0.1 vs 0.92 in 2D. n=5 maps beat n=1 and n=10 (SR 0.92 vs 0.86/0.88). PReLU beats ReLU (figure only). PCA of instruction embeddings shows attribute vector-arithmetic structure, which fits the higher zero-shot success.
method: Input processing: 4-layer CNN on 84x84x3 RGB (bird's-eye in 2D, egocentric in 3D) gives a WxHxD feature volume; the instruction is one-hot encoded, passed through a GRU (size 16), and the final output goes through n parallel FC layers (size 64) giving V_1..V_n.

Multimodal fusion (A3C_attn): each V_j acts as a 1x1 conv filter over the visual volume, giving n WxHx1 attention maps that are concatenated into a WxHxn tensor; two extra 3x3 conv layers follow. n in {1,5,10}.
Variant A3C_netattn: concatenates one attention map with the visual representation (WxHx(D+1)).
Policy learning: A3C with an LSTM (32), a 4-way policy head and a value head, PReLU activations, Adam (lr 1e-4, decayed by 0.9 every 10k steps), 32 threads, gamma 0.99, GAE, entropy regularization.

Custom 2D grid environment: 10x10 grid, 63 objects with color/size attributes, 8 obstacles, 3-18 word instructions, 72-word vocabulary, rewards +1 target / -1 wall / -0.5 wrong object, limited-radius view.
3D VizDoom: the Chaplot et al. environment and hyperparameters, with the Hadamard fusion replaced by the attention fusion, trained from scratch.
Translation by-product: English and French decoders on top of the GRU embedding are trained to reconstruct the instruction; at test time the decoders are swapped to translate.

setting.backbone: CNN + GRU + attention fusion + LSTM A3C (trained from scratch)
setting.training_data: RL in a self-made 2D grid world (random scenarios, 3-6 objects from 63, 19 held-out instructions for zero-shot) and the VizDoom language-grounding environment of Chaplot et al.; no external data
setting.observation: raw RGB pixels (84x84x3): limited-radius bird's-eye view in 2D, egocentric view in 3D, plus a natural-language instruction
setting.action_space: 2D: discrete up/down/left/right; 3D: VizDoom discrete movement actions (as in Chaplot et al.)

numbers.eval_set_note: averaged over 100 episodes, unseen scenarios with training instructions
numbers.extra: RL from scratch; success rate in ZS column is for 19 held-out instructions (mean reward)
numbers.evidence: Table 1: A3C_attn (n=5) 0.95 / 0.8 / 0.92; Table 2: 0.95 mean reward, 0.92 success rate

numbers.extra: US = unseen scenario, ZS = zero-shot instructions

numbers_note: No standard VLN/navigation benchmark is used; metrics are on the authors' own 2D grid and the VizDoom language-grounding task. Values are printed as fractions. Training curves and the PReLU vs ReLU ablation appear only in figures.
results: In 2D, A3C_attn (n=5) reaches SR 0.92 and mean reward 0.95, against Hadamard 0.5 / 0.4 and concatenation 0.1 / -2.9. In 3D VizDoom it beats Hadamard on all zero-shot splits (Hard ZS 0.83 vs 0.73) and converges faster. The learned embeddings support vector arithmetic, and unsupervised English-French translation reaches 85% exact match.
limitations: Evaluation is on simple synthetic environments (a custom 2D grid and VizDoom), with only 100 evaluation episodes and no variance reported.
Small vocabulary (72 words) and templated instructions; the zero-shot test consists of only 19 held-out instructions.
No comparison with the standard photo-realistic VLN benchmarks; the 3D hard-case numbers are still below perfect.
